Chokepoint Watch: Aerospace and Defence
Weekly theme watch · evidence, not a trade

Chokepoint Watch: Aerospace and Defence

As of 2026-10-19Edition 1Previous edition: first edition

Engines, airframes and defence electronics. Munitions, energetics and rocket motors are out of scope.

This is edition 1. No earlier artifact with this title exists, so nothing is carried forward and no predictions are due.

What changedFirst edition. GE Aerospace agreed on 2026-09-08 to buy castings maker CPP for $11.75bn, saying casting capacity "is needed" for demand. That is customer-funded capacity at the casting layer.
Top chokepointaer-1: engine airfoil and structural investment castings (Howmet, PCC, CPP, DPC). Scarcity is supported by primary sources in direction but not in units. Capture is unproven.
Next datedGE Aerospace and RTX Q3 2026 results on 2026-10-20. Then Safran Q3 revenue on 10-23 and Howmet Q3 on 10-29.

Marks: P primary, L lead, map own knowledge, used only to draw the chain. Step states: primary lead unexamined contradicted.

2Predictions settled this week

None. This is the first edition, so no predictions exist yet.

3The board

Two chokepoints are named and both get a deep dive. The other candidates did not reach primary evidence in this run (see Rejected).

aer-1 · layer: casting (investment-cast airfoils and structural castings) · status: new

Nickel-superalloy and titanium investment castings for engines

The chain

  1. Aircraft makers raise narrowbody rates, and so engine deliveries rise. Safran: LEAP deliveries "reached 1,030 units, representing a 41% increase compared to the first half of 2025." P
  2. Engine OEMs guide higher: LEAP "up high-teens (previously ~15%)" (Safran), "with LEAP deliveries up high teens from 15% previously" (GE). P (engine layer)
  3. Aftermarket: GE reports "spare parts delinquency, which represents shipments that have been delayed due to material availability constraints". P (spare-part layer; castings not named)
  4. Engine to casting: hot-section blades and vanes, and structural castings, are investment-cast by a small group of qualified foundries. map
  5. Casting layer: GE says "Investing in mission-critical casting capacity is needed to support the strong simultaneous demand across commercial engines, aftermarket and defense." P
  6. Holders: Howmet (listed), PCC (Berkshire Hathaway), CPP (being bought by GE) and DPC. Fool says these four "dominate the casting space." L
StepStateEvidence
Constraintlead

No source gives a shortfall in parts a month or engines a year. GE ties delayed spares to "material availability constraints", but does not name castings in the part of the call that was read. Howmet's "We have one casting pit left" reached this run only through a fetch-tool summary, so it is downgraded to a lead here (the Council had cited it as P via Power Equipment).

"spare parts delinquency, which represents shipments that have been delayed due to material availability constraints"Rahul Ghai, CFO, GE Aerospace · Q2 2026 earnings call · 2026-07-16 · gloom.sh transcript · verbatim page text (machine transcript)
Demand vs supplyprimary

Money committed at the casting layer. This is customer-funded capacity, the strongest kind of evidence. The engine OEM is paying to own the capacity, and the holder is spending more capex.

"Purchase price of $11.75 billion to be financed with $7 billion in cash, with the remainder in new debt."GE Aerospace · press release, Ex. 99.2 to 8-K · 2026-09-08 · SEC · verbatim
"Investing in mission-critical casting capacity is needed to support the strong simultaneous demand across commercial engines, aftermarket and defense."H. Lawrence Culp Jr., CEO, GE Aerospace · same release · geaerospace.com · verbatim
"...while this year, we are now likely to exceed $500 million in capital spend, we are already seeing the need to further increase this in 2027."John Plant, CEO, Howmet · Q2 2026 call · 2026-08-06 · fool.com · verbatim

The GE deck shows "Growing airfoil demand > 30 % growth" (Ex. 99.1, slide text, P). Defence demand: CPP is "~20% Defense" by revenue (Ex. 99.1). That demand is funded but not broken out by programme. Howmet's Engine Products revenue rose 32% y/y in Q2 2026 (release, P), which shows output rising, not a shortfall.

Reliefprimary

New capacity is coming but is slow. The CPP deal "is expected to close in the second half of 2027" (GE release, P), and GE plans "incremental planned capital investments over time" (IR update, P). Howmet cites "the new plant we built in Japan, the major expansion in Europe" and freed space in Virginia, and Plant signed off "the building of a new plant" (Q2 call, P). Customer qualification and first-article approval of new casting lines usually take 1–2 years. map, not evidence.

Controllead

Four holders per press (Fool, 2026-09-27). No share figures were found in a primary source this run. CPP: "~$2.0B '27E revenue", "~70% of revenue from commercial and defense engines" (GE Ex. 99.1, P), "~6,600 employees across more than 20 facilities" (release, P). Howmet Engine Products: $1.37bn Q2 2026 revenue (release, P). PCC and DPC: unexamined. The Berkshire 10-Q could not be reached.

Captureunexamined

No price increase was found in the seller's own words this run. Howmet's only pricing-adjacent line is pass-through: "Higher metal pass-through diluted margins by approximately 360 basis points year-over-year, but had no material impact on EBITDA dollars." (Winterlich, Q2 call, P). The valuation GE pays, "~18x 2027 EBITDA including expected net synergies, multiple of ~26x without" (release, P), signals what the buyer thinks the capacity is worth. It is not pricing evidence. Cost share: castings are probably a low-single-digit percent of an engine's cost (estimate). With no substitute, that favours price over redesign.

Invalidationprimary
"nine consecutive quarters with double-digit increases from our critical suppliers"Larry Culp · GE Q2 2026 call · 2026-07-16 · gloom.sh · verbatim (machine transcript)

Supplier input keeps rising quarter after quarter, which argues for relief in progress. In the verbatim half of RTX's Q2 call, no castings or forgings constraint is named. Safran's H1 release names only "supply chain production capabilities" as a watch item. GE says CPP is "a part of the solution, but we will continue to need all our partners and suppliers" (IR update, P), which is ambiguous.

Physical scarcity

Supported in direction (P: customer-funded capacity, rising capex, spares delayed by material). Not quantified, and no source names castings as today's binding limit.

Economic capture

Unproven. Sales to engine OEMs are usually long-term fixed-price agreements with metal pass-through map. No price-increase quote this run.

Investability

Howmet is listed and is the only independent holder that is. CPP becomes captive to GE. PCC is captive in Berkshire. DPC is private.

Bear checks

  • Dilution: GE is financing with cash and debt and names no equity issue (P). Howmet's dilution was not examined.
  • Margins: metal pass-through cut Howmet's margin by about 360bp (P). No fixed-price losses were found.
  • Concentration: CPP is a "Key supplier to key GE Aerospace programs… LEAP, GEnx, T700, F110, F404" (Ex. 99.1, P). Concentration on LEAP is high.
  • Second source: GE in-sourcing CPP may cut GE's buying from Howmet over time, or may tighten supply for other OEMs. Neither effect is evidenced.
  • Design bypass: CMC parts replace some superalloy hot-section parts in new engines map. That is slow and not a 36-month relief.
  • Rate cuts: airframe rate risk was not examined this run.
  • Budget: about 20% of CPP is defence. No CR or appropriations exposure was checked.
  • Layer error: GE's "material availability" covers all supplier material, not castings alone. It supports the spare-part layer, not the casting layer.

Kill criteria

  • GE or RTX Q3 2026 materials (2026-10-20) or Q4 2026 materials (late Jan 2027) report spare-parts delinquency falling with supplier material input meeting demand.
  • Howmet Q3 2026 (2026-10-29) or Q4 2026 reports unused engine casting capacity, a capex cut or price concessions.
  • The GE–CPP deal is terminated without GE announcing other casting capacity.
  • Safran or GE cut 2027 LEAP delivery guidance for reasons other than castings.

aer-p2 · made 2026-10-19 · deadline 2027-04-19 · openBy 2027-04-19, GE Aerospace's FY2026 Form 10-K will name casting capacity or supplier material availability as a factor limiting engine deliveries or spare-parts output, as shown by the 10-K risk factors or MD&A.
Status
New.
Consensus
Earliest primary evidence in this run: 2026-07-16 (GE Q2 call). It is emerging: the CPP deal was widely reported, but the press framed it as a capacity purchase, not as a castings shortage with figures.
aer-2 · layer: rare-earth oxide/metal → SmCo alloy → magnet · status: new

Samarium feedstock outside China for samarium-cobalt magnets, ahead of the 2027 DFARS cliff

The chain

  1. US military aircraft and defence electronics programmes use SmCo magnets in actuators, motors, sensors and RF tubes. map
  2. DFARS 252.225-7052 lists "Samarium-cobalt magnets" as covered material, and China is a covered country. P
  3. From 2027-01-01, the rule covers "the entire supply chain from mining or production of a cobalt and samarium ore or feedstock, including recycled material, through production of finished magnets." P (feedstock layer)
  4. China controls samarium exports: in April 2025 it added "specific controls on alloys, compounds, metals, and oxides of samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium..." (USGS MCS 2026). P
  5. Magnet layer: EEC (Permag group) calls itself "the only US-based producer of samarium cobalt (SmCo) magnets". P (self-claim)
  6. Feedstock outside China: magnet makers "are in negotiations to work with suppliers outside of China" (Permag, 2025). Ucore is developing samarium separation with DoW funding. P
StepStateEvidence
Constraintlead

The constraint is regulatory-physical: DFARS-compliant samarium oxide or metal from 2027-01-01. No primary source gives tonnes of shortfall. Adamas (2026-06-05), citing an unlinked FT report, says contractors argue "a substantial supply gap remains because no Western alternative has yet scaled to required volumes" L.

Demand vs supplylead
"In addition to the materials listed below, the fiscal year (FY) 2025 potential acquisitions included 300 tons of neodymium-praseodymium oxide, 450 tons of neodymium-iron-boron magnet block, and 60 tons of samarium-cobalt alloy."USGS · Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Rare Earths · Feb 2026 · USGS PDF · verbatim (text conversion)

The 60 t is a stockpile potential acquisition. That is a stated plan, not an award. Defence demand comes from the sourcing mandate, not from a quantified order book.

Reliefprimary
"The additional funding supports samarium ("Sm") and gadolinium ("Gd") process development"Ucore Rare Metals · release (via INN) · 2026-09-14 · investingnews.com · verbatim excerpt

The OTA now totals US$27.0m, through "U.S. Army Contracting Command-Orlando" (P). It gives no tonnage or start date. A regulatory relief valve also exists in the clause: a nonavailability determination that compliant material "cannot be procured as and when needed at a reasonable price" (DFARS (c)(2), P). The magnet layer is expanding too: EEC's plan "more than doubles its production capacity" (Permag, 2025-08-22, P). That relieves the magnet layer, not the feedstock layer.

Controllead

Feedstock: TechSpot (2025-12-24, summarising the NYT) says "China supplies nearly all of the world's samarium" L. Non-China supply named in press: a Solvay stockpile in France, processed by Less Common Metals in the UK L. Magnet: EEC is the sole US producer (self-claim, P). European SmCo makers were not examined.

Capturelead

Official statistics show samarium oxide (99.5%, FOB China, Argus) at $2.01/kg in 2024 and $2.82/kg in 2025e (USGS table, P). That is a rise of about 40%, but it is the Chinese price, not the price of compliant supply outside China, which was not found. Cost share: magnets are a tiny fraction of a system's cost (estimate), so buyers will pay rather than redesign. The economics would sit with private or pre-revenue firms.

Invalidationprimary

The clause exempts COTS end items under 50% covered material by weight, and "An electronic device, unless otherwise specified in the contract" (DFARS (c)(1)(iii), P). That narrows the demand the cliff hits. The magnet makers targeted compliance "by mid-2026" and are "actively working with compliant global suppliers" (Permag, 2025, P), which implies they have a route. USGS: "China began to issue general export licenses to selected exporters" (P). That eases supply before 2027, but Chinese-mined material is non-compliant from 2027.

Physical scarcity

Lead. A dated regulatory cliff (P) meets feedstock dominated by China (L). No tonnage gap is shown in a primary source.

Economic capture

Unproven. Price evidence covers only Chinese oxide. Defence buyers pay through cost-plus development and fixed-price production. The contract mix was not examined.

Investability

Weak. The magnet holder is private (Permag group). Ucore is small, grant-funded and likely to dilute (unexamined). Solvay's samarium is immaterial to the group.

Bear checks

  • Dilution: Ucore is pre-revenue (unexamined). EEC is private.
  • Second source: DoW-funded entrants (Ucore, Louisiana) are qualifying. Timing is undisclosed.
  • Design bypass: NdFeB with heavy rare earths can replace SmCo in lower-temperature uses map. NdFeB faces the same 2027 rule.
  • Budget: stockpile figures for FY2026 are "not available" (USGS, P). The Annual Materials Plan was not released.
  • Policy delay: the strongest bear case. Contractors are lobbying to postpone the 2027 date (Adamas, L). The eCFR, current through 2026-10-15, still shows "Effective January 1, 2027" (P).
  • Layer error: the stockpile line is SmCo alloy, not oxide. The price line is oxide.

Kill criteria

  • A Federal Register notice, DFARS class deviation or statute delays the 2027-01-01 supply-chain provision for SmCo magnets.
  • Broad nonavailability determinations are published for SmCo magnets.
  • A magnet maker or prime announces contracted DFARS-compliant samarium supply covering its 2027 needs.
aer-p3 · made 2026-10-19 · deadline 2027-01-15 · openBy 2027-01-15, the eCFR text of DFARS 252.225-7052 will still contain the "Effective January 1, 2027" supply-chain restriction for samarium-cobalt magnets with no delay, as shown by the eCFR or the Federal Register.
aer-p4 · made 2026-10-19 · deadline 2027-04-19 · openBy 2027-04-19, the Department of War or DLA will announce at least one new award (contract, OTA or DPA Title III) whose stated purpose includes samarium oxide, samarium metal or SmCo magnet production, as shown by a DoW contract announcement, DLA notice or the awardee's release.
Status
New.
Consensus
Earliest primary evidence: the April 2025 Chinese controls (as reported by USGS, Feb 2026) and the DFARS clause (May 2024). It is emerging: NYT, FT and trade press cover it, and financial-analyst coverage is thin.

CandidateReason
Large closed-die and isothermal forgings (presses)Not examined this run, and no primary evidence was gathered. Reopen next week from Howmet Q3 and PCC.
GKN fan cases (part layer)GE names GKN "to break constraints tied to rate performance" (GE Q2 call, P). That is one supplier's performance problem, not missing qualified capacity. Moved to next questions.
Pratt & Whitney powder metalThe only verbatim reference is "powder metal-related compensation was approximately $150 million" (RTX Q2 call, 2026-07-23, P). That is a quality-recall cost, not a capacity constraint.

GaN and GaAs for radarNo evidence was gathered this run. The Council question on quantified demand went unanswered (see below).
Tb/Dy NdFeB magnetsCarried by Robotics (rob-1). The defence side is quantified only as a 450 t stockpile potential acquisition (USGS, P). It is not named separately here to avoid double counting.
Munitions, rocket motors, energeticsOut of scope. RTX's Q2 call mentions munitions output and European AMRAAM suppliers. Noted only.

5Cross-theme hooks

  • Investment castings (Howmet, CPP, PCC): shared with Power Equipment's IGT blades (pwr-2). CPP is "~20% Power and other" and Howmet allocates one capex pool to both (Council cst-1).
  • DFARS 252.225-7052 magnet rule, 2027-01-01: it covers NdFeB as well as SmCo, so Robotics (rob-1) faces the same supply-chain cliff in defence-adjacent demand.
  • Chinese rare-earth and minor-metal export controls: the April 2025 list (Sm, Gd, Tb, Dy...) sits beside the Ga/Ge controls that Photonics tracks. Licence changes move several themes at once.

It attributes delayed spares to "material availability constraints" without naming castings in the part of its Q2 call that was read. RTX's verbatim Q2 text names no castings or forgings. Safran's H1 release names only "supply chain production capabilities". The Q3 releases are not out yet: GE and RTX report 10-20, Safran 10-23.P partial
Is Tb/Dy NdFeB or GaAs/GaN defence demand quantified in government documents (cst-2, cst-3)?NdFeB: partly. The FY2025 stockpile potential acquisitions included 450 t of NdFeB magnet block and 60 t of SmCo alloy. They are not Tb/Dy-specific, and FY2026 figures were "not available" (USGS MCS 2026). GaAs/GaN: not found.P NdFeB · not found GaAs/GaN

7Next questions

  • Do GE and RTX name castings, forgings or a specific supplier in Q3 2026 results, and is GE's spare-parts delinquency rising or falling? Where: GE and RTX Q3 releases and calls, 2026-10-20.
  • Has Safran's "supply chain production capabilities" watch item changed, and does it name parts? Where: Safran Q3 revenue release, 2026-10-23.
  • What is Howmet's capacity and pricing, how does it split aero and IGT, and does it comment on GE–CPP? Where: Howmet Q3 release and call, 2026-10-29.
  • Has any DFARS 252.225-7052 delay, class deviation or nonavailability determination been published, and what came of the DIBC's February 2026 request on samarium? Where: Federal Register, DPC class deviations, DIBC and DoW releases.
  • What is the forging-press layer (PCC Wyman-Gordon, Howmet) and GKN's fan-case constraint? Where: Melrose H1 2026 results, Berkshire 10-Q (by another route), Howmet Q3.

8Run notes

  • Unreachable: SEC EDGAR company browse (robots), so there is no Berkshire 10-Q or PCC text. The defense.gov releases list was also blocked by robots. The National Defense Magazine article returned empty. Globe and Mail was blocked by robots, and the Fool GE transcript URL failed.
  • Truncated transcripts: GE (gloom.sh, about 66% read verbatim), RTX (Fool, about 49%) and Howmet (Fool, about 54%). Q&A sections were mostly unread. Text from the summarised parts was not used as P.
  • Downgraded to lead: Howmet's "one casting pit left" (summary only this run); Howmet's "sold out" remark (garbled transcription); GE's "We do not have a demand problem" (summary only).
  • Source caveats: the GE transcript is machine-transcribed, with name errors. The Permag DFARS release shows two dates (20 May and 12 June 2025). GE's Q3 date (2026-10-20) comes from a third party (24/7 Wall St via Yahoo, 2026-10-19), and GE's IR site shows no date. The SEC 8-K filing date was not confirmed. Some fetched pages carried embedded instruction text, which was ignored.
  • Copies: the GE CPP release on SEC and on geaerospace.com count as one source.
  • Tool calls: about 30 (artifact list and read, 9 searches, 9 fetch agents making about 50 page fetches, skill load, publish).
